newsitem.title: FRANCE: French parties kick off snap election debate.
newsitem.headline: French parties kick off snap election debate.

text.p: French politicians waded into the first day of campaigning for a snap parliamentary election on Tuesday with the opposition Socialists charging President Jacques Chirac wanted to make France a more unjust society.
In a high-stakes gamble that could make or break his presidency, Chirac dissolved the National Assembly on Monday and brought forward the election by 10 months to May 25 and June 1.
The timetable seemed calculated to keep the campaign as short as possible, with barely a month -- littered with public holidays and major sports events -- before the first round of voting.

Chirac said the early poll was needed to prepare France for a single European currency and give his centre-right coalition a five-year mandate to reform the state, reduce public spending and cut taxes and welfare charges.

French financial markets, which fell on the prospect of an uncertain early election, began to rally on Tuesday. The franc and bonds were stronger on the view that the conservatives were likely to keep a comfortable majority, dealers said.
But former Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius said the decision could yet backfire on the conservative president.

"Will the French say 'bravo' to the rise in unemployment, 'great' to the rise in taxes, 'well done' for the increase in poverty? I doubt it," the Socialist parliamentary floor leader told Europe 1 radio.
He said the left had a 50-50 chance of victory.

Former Socialist labour minister Martine Aubry said the poll gave French voters a choice between two models of society -- one more market-dominated, with less social protection, more poverty and social exclusion, the other more equal and fairer.
Chirac's supporters rallied to defend his decision. Prime Minister Alain Juppe was due to set out the ruling coalition's election platform in a keynote speech at 3.30 p.m. (1330 GMT).

Jean-Francois Mancel, secretary general of Chirac's Gaullist RPR party, said the dissolution was in the national interest and denounced as "brazen lies" accusations it was a ploy to pave the way for a new bout of harsher austerity and hide the government's failings behind a rushed campaign.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said on Monday night that Chirac was veering towards a harsher Anglo-Saxon brand of capitalism. Far-right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen accused Chirac of an "electoral hold-up, a shameful swindle".
Victory would ensure the 64-year-old president a renewed, if sharply reduced, majority in parliament for the remaining five years of his presidency.
But defeat could reduce him to a lame duck overshadowed by a prime minister Jospin.
"It's a serious game of poker," said Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais. "The outcome is far from a foregone conclusion."
The main worry for French voters is unemployment -- which has risen to 12.8 percent of the workforce from 11.7 percent when Chirac took office two years ago promising a war for jobs.

The president cited the need to approach European economic and monetary union from a position of strength as a key reason for the early poll. The European Union will decide early in 1998 which nations qualify for a single currency.
Jospin said the Socialists too favour the single currency -- but not at the price of an extra bout of austerity.
He also said the government wanted a quick poll before corruption scandals engulfed some of its leading members.

Opinion polls taken before Chirac's announcement showed that the centre-right, which now has 464 members out of 577 seats in the National Assembly, could lose about 150 seats but still retain a majority. The coalition also has about a dozen allies in parliament.
